chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Nest (NestJS) is a framework for building efficient, scalable Node.js server-side applications.

chapters.title: First steps
chapters.summary: This set of articles covers the core fundamentals of Nest.

chapters.title: Controllers
chapters.summary: Controllers are responsible for handling incoming requests and sending responses back to the client.

chapters.title: Providers
chapters.summary: Providers are a core concept in Nest.

chapters.title: Modules
chapters.summary: A module is a class annotated with the @Module() decorator.

chapters.title: Middleware
chapters.summary: Middleware is a function that is called before the route handler.

chapters.title: Exception filters
chapters.summary: Nest comes with a built-in exceptions layer that processes all unhandled exceptions across an application.

chapters.title: Pipes
chapters.summary: A pipe is a class annotated with the @Injectable() decorator that implements the PipeTransform interface.

chapters.title: Guards
chapters.summary: A guard is a class annotated with the @Injectable() decorator that implements the CanActivate interface.

chapters.title: Interceptors
chapters.summary: An interceptor is a class annotated with the @Injectable() decorator that implements the NestInterceptor interface.

chapters.title: Custom decorators
chapters.summary: Nest is built around a language feature called decorators.

chapters.title: Custom providers
chapters.summary: Earlier chapters touched on various aspects of dependency injection (DI) and how Nest uses it.

chapters.title: Asynchronous providers
chapters.summary: Sometimes the application start should be delayed until one or more asynchronous tasks complete.

chapters.title: Dynamic modules
chapters.summary: The Modules chapter covers the basics of Nest modules and includes a brief introduction to dynamic modules.

chapters.title: Injection scopes
chapters.summary: If you come from a different programming language background, you might be surprised to learn that in Nest, almost everything is shared across incoming requests: a connection pool to the database, singleton services with global state, and so on.

chapters.title: Circular dependency
chapters.summary: A circular dependency occurs when two classes depend on each other.

chapters.title: Module reference
chapters.summary: Nest provides the ModuleRef class to navigate the internal list of providers and obtain a reference to any provider, using its injection token as a lookup key.

chapters.title: Lazy-loading modules
chapters.summary: By default, modules are eagerly loaded: as soon as the application loads, so do all the modules, whether or not they are immediately needed.

chapters.title: Execution context
chapters.summary: Nest provides several utility classes that help you write applications that function across multiple application contexts (e.g., HTTP server-based, microservices, and WebSockets application contexts).

chapters.title: Lifecycle events
chapters.summary: A Nest application, as well as every application element, has a lifecycle managed by Nest.

chapters.title: Discovery service
chapters.summary: The DiscoveryService, provided by the @nestjs/core package, lets you dynamically inspect and retrieve providers, controllers, and their metadata within a NestJS application.

chapters.title: Platform agnosticism
chapters.summary: Nest is a platform-agnostic framework.

chapters.title: Testing
chapters.summary: Automated testing is an essential part of any serious software development effort.

chapters.title: Configuration
chapters.summary: Applications often run in different environments, and each environment needs its own configuration settings.

chapters.title: Validation
chapters.summary: Validate every piece of data a web application receives before acting on it.

chapters.title: Serialization
chapters.summary: Serialization happens before objects are returned in a network response.

chapters.title: Logging
chapters.summary: Nest comes with a built-in logger that is used during application bootstrapping and in several other circumstances, such as displaying caught exceptions (i.e., system logging).

chapters.title: Events
chapters.summary: The Event Emitter package (@nestjs/event-emitter) provides an observer implementation that lets you subscribe to and listen for events that occur in your application.

chapters.title: Task scheduling
chapters.summary: Task scheduling lets you run arbitrary code (methods or functions) at a fixed date and time, at recurring intervals, or once after a specified delay.

chapters.title: Queues
chapters.summary: Queues are a design pattern that helps you deal with common application scaling and performance challenges.

chapters.title: HTTP client
chapters.summary: Most applications call other services over HTTP.

chapters.title: Internationalization
chapters.summary: An online store for cat food and supplies sells to customers in the United States, Poland and Germany, and its order API should answer each of them in their own language.

chapters.title: Mail
chapters.summary: When a customer places an order at an online store for cat food and supplies, they expect a confirmation email within a minute: the items, the total, a link to the order, and the invoice as a PDF.

chapters.title: File storage
chapters.summary: An online store for cat food and supplies keeps three kinds of files.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.summary: Nest is database-agnostic, so you can integrate it with any SQL or NoSQL database.

chapters.title: TypeORM
chapters.summary: The @nestjs/typeorm package integrates TypeORM with Nest.

chapters.title: Drizzle
chapters.summary: As an alternative to TypeORM, you can use Drizzle ORM with the @nestjs/drizzle package.

chapters.title: MongoDB
chapters.summary: Nest supports two methods for integrating with the MongoDB database.

chapters.title: Prisma
chapters.summary: Prisma is an open-source ORM for Node.js and TypeScript.

chapters.title: MikroORM
chapters.summary: MikroORM is a TypeScript ORM for Node.js based on the Data Mapper, Unit of Work, and Identity Map patterns.

chapters.title: Sequelize
chapters.summary: The @nestjs/sequelize package integrates the Sequelize ORM with Nest.

chapters.title: Caching
chapters.summary: Caching is a straightforward and effective technique for improving your application's performance.

chapters.title: Authentication
chapters.summary: @nestjs/authentication signs users in and tells the rest of your application who they are.

chapters.title: Authorization
chapters.summary: @nestjs/authorization expresses permissions as policies: classes whose methods answer "may this user do this?".

chapters.title: Encryption and Hashing
chapters.summary: Encryption is the process of encoding information.

chapters.title: Security headers
chapters.summary: Security headers, such as the ones Helmet sets, tell browsers to turn on protections against well-known web attacks like cross-site scripting and clickjacking.

chapters.title: CORS
chapters.summary: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) is a mechanism that allows resources to be requested from another domain.

chapters.title: CSRF Protection
chapters.summary: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF or XSRF) is an attack in which a malicious site makes a user's browser send unwanted, state-changing requests to your application.

chapters.title: Rate limiting
chapters.summary: A common technique to protect applications from brute-force attacks is rate limiting.

chapters.title: Versioning
chapters.summary: Versioning lets you run different versions of your controllers or individual routes within the same application.

chapters.title: Cookies
chapters.summary: An HTTP cookie is a small piece of data that the user's browser stores.

chapters.title: Session
chapters.summary: HTTP sessions store information about the user across multiple requests, which is particularly useful for MVC applications.

chapters.title: File upload and streaming
chapters.summary: This chapter covers files in both directions: receiving files that clients upload, and streaming files back to clients.

chapters.title: Compression
chapters.summary: Compression can significantly reduce the size of the response body, which makes a web app faster to load.

chapters.title: Server-Sent Events
chapters.summary: Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a server push technology that enables a client to receive automatic updates from a server over an HTTP connection.

chapters.title: Model-View-Controller
chapters.summary: By default, Nest uses the Express library under the hood.

chapters.title: Performance (Fastify)
chapters.summary: By default, Nest uses the Express framework.

chapters.title: Webhooks
chapters.summary: An online store for cat food and supplies sells to cat shelters and resellers that buy in bulk, through its API.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.summary: NestJS Observe is the official, auto-instrumented application performance monitoring (APM) and observability platform for NestJS applications.

chapters.title: SDK
chapters.summary: The @nestjs/observe SDK is what gets your application's requests, jobs, errors, logs, and traces into your NestJS Observe dashboard.

chapters.title: Manual instrumentation
chapters.summary: Most of the SDK is automatic instrumentation: you configure it once and it decides what to record.

chapters.title: Distributed tracing
chapters.summary: A trace is everything your applications recorded under a single trace id: the request or job that started it, and every span underneath.

chapters.title: Error monitoring
chapters.summary: Error monitoring is included in every NestJS Observe plan, Free included, and needs nothing beyond the SDK.

chapters.title: Dashboard
chapters.summary: Once an application is instrumented and sending data, its project dashboard fills in automatically, with no queries to write and no dashboards to build.

chapters.title: MCP server
chapters.summary: NestJS Observe exposes an MCP server, so an MCP-compatible client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, or an agent you wrote yourself) can query your projects directly instead of you copying dashboard data into a prompt.

chapters.title: OpenTelemetry
chapters.summary: OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for traces, metrics, and logs.

chapters.title: Resilience
chapters.summary: Sooner or later, every application that calls another system meets one that is slow or down.

chapters.title: Idempotency keys
chapters.summary: A customer of an online store for cat food and supplies pays for salmon kibble and cat litter in the store's mobile app, on a phone on a train.

chapters.title: Transactional outbox
chapters.summary: When a customer places an order at an online store for cat food and supplies, the order API saves the order and announces it with an OrderPlaced event.

chapters.title: Durable workflows
chapters.summary: Some business processes take days and span several systems.

chapters.title: Distributed locks
chapters.summary: An online store for cat food and supplies runs two scheduled jobs with @nestjs/schedule.

chapters.title: Health checks
chapters.summary: The Terminus integration provides readiness/liveness health checks.

chapters.title: Quick start
chapters.summary: GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for fulfilling those queries with your existing data.

chapters.title: Resolvers
chapters.summary: Resolvers provide the instructions for turning a GraphQL operation (a query, mutation, or subscription) into data.

chapters.title: Mutations
chapters.summary: Most discussions of GraphQL focus on data fetching, but any complete data platform needs a way to modify server-side data as well.

chapters.title: Subscriptions
chapters.summary: In addition to fetching data with queries and modifying data with mutations, the GraphQL spec supports a third operation type, called subscription.

chapters.title: Scalars
chapters.summary: A GraphQL object type has a name and fields, but at some point those fields have to resolve to some concrete data.

chapters.title: Directives
chapters.summary: A directive can be attached to a field or fragment inclusion, and can affect execution of the query in any way the server desires (see directives in the GraphQL documentation).

chapters.title: Interfaces
chapters.summary: Like many type systems, GraphQL supports interfaces.

chapters.title: Unions and Enums
chapters.summary: Union types are similar to interfaces, but they don't specify any common fields between the types (see union types in the GraphQL documentation).

chapters.title: Field middleware
chapters.summary: Field middleware lets you run arbitrary code before or after a field is resolved.

chapters.title: Mapped types
chapters.summary: As you build out features like CRUD (Create/Read/Update/Delete), it's often useful to construct variants of a base entity type.

chapters.title: Plugins
chapters.summary: Plugins let you extend Apollo Server's core functionality by performing custom operations in response to certain events.

chapters.title: Complexity
chapters.summary: Query complexity lets you define how complex certain fields are, and restrict queries with a maximum complexity.

chapters.title: Extensions
chapters.summary: Extensions are an advanced, low-level feature that lets you define arbitrary data in the types configuration.

chapters.title: CLI Plugin
chapters.summary: TypeScript's metadata reflection system has several limitations that make it impossible to, for instance, determine which properties a class consists of, or whether a given property is optional or required.

chapters.title: Generating SDL
chapters.summary: To generate a GraphQL SDL schema manually (i.e., without running an application, connecting to the database, hooking up resolvers, etc.), use the GraphQLSchemaBuilderModule:.

chapters.title: Sharing models
chapters.summary: One of the biggest advantages of using TypeScript for the backend of your project is the ability to reuse the same models in a TypeScript-based frontend application through a common TypeScript package.

chapters.title: Other features
chapters.summary: In the GraphQL world, there is a lot of debate about handling concerns like authentication or the side effects of operations.

chapters.title: Federation
chapters.summary: Federation lets you split a monolithic GraphQL server into independent microservices.

chapters.title: Gateways
chapters.summary: Most of the concepts discussed elsewhere in this documentation, such as dependency injection, decorators, exception filters, pipes, guards, and interceptors, apply equally to gateways.

chapters.title: Exception filters
chapters.summary: The WebSockets exceptions layer works like the HTTP exception filter layer, with one difference: instead of throwing HttpException, throw WsException.

chapters.title: Pipes
chapters.summary: There is no fundamental difference between regular pipes and WebSocket pipes.

chapters.title: Guards
chapters.summary: There is no fundamental difference between WebSocket guards and regular HTTP application guards.

chapters.title: Interceptors
chapters.summary: There is no difference between regular interceptors and WebSocket interceptors.

chapters.title: Adapters
chapters.summary: The WebSockets module is platform-agnostic, so you can bring your own library (or even a native implementation) by implementing the WebSocketAdapter interface.

chapters.title: Overview
chapters.summary: In addition to traditional (sometimes called monolithic) application architectures, Nest natively supports the microservice architectural style of development.

chapters.title: Redis
chapters.summary: The Redis transporter implements the publish/subscribe messaging paradigm and uses the Pub/Sub feature of Redis.

chapters.title: MQTT
chapters.summary: MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) is an open source, lightweight messaging protocol optimized for low latency.

chapters.title: NATS
chapters.summary: NATS is a simple, secure, and high-performance open source messaging system for cloud native applications, IoT messaging, and microservices architectures.

chapters.title: RabbitMQ
chapters.summary: RabbitMQ is an open-source, lightweight message broker that supports multiple messaging protocols.

chapters.title: Kafka
chapters.summary: Kafka is an open source, distributed streaming platform with three key capabilities:.

chapters.title: gRPC
chapters.summary: gRPC is a modern, open source, high-performance RPC framework that can run in any environment.

chapters.title: Custom transporters
chapters.summary: Nest provides a variety of transporters out of the box, as well as an API for building custom transport strategies.

chapters.title: Exception filters
chapters.summary: The only difference between the HTTP exception filter layer and the corresponding microservices layer is that microservices should throw RpcException instead of HttpException.

chapters.title: Pipes
chapters.summary: Microservice pipes work the same way as regular pipes.

chapters.title: Pre-request hooks
chapters.summary: Pre-request hooks are functions that run before all enhancers (guards, interceptors, and pipes) on every invocation of a pattern handler.

chapters.title: Guards
chapters.summary: Microservice guards work the same way as regular HTTP application guards.

chapters.title: Interceptors
chapters.summary: Microservice interceptors work the same way as regular interceptors.

chapters.summary: When you're ready to deploy your NestJS application to production, there are key steps you can take to ensure it runs as efficiently as possible.

chapters.title: CRUD generator

chapters.summary: Passport is the most popular Node.js authentication library, well known in the community and used in many production applications.

chapters.title: Commander
chapters.summary: Expanding on the standalone applications chapter, the nest-commander package lets you write command-line applications with a structure similar to a typical Nest application.

chapters.title: Async local storage
chapters.summary: AsyncLocalStorage is a Node.js API (based on the asynchooks API) that provides an alternative way of propagating local state through the application without explicitly passing it as a function parameter.

chapters.title: Serverless

chapters.summary: Occasionally, you may need to access the underlying HTTP server, either from within the Nest application context or from outside of it.

chapters.title: Keep-Alive connections
chapters.summary: By default, the NestJS HTTP adapters wait until responses have finished before closing the application.

chapters.title: Global path prefix
chapters.summary: To set a prefix for every route registered in an HTTP application, call the setGlobalPrefix() method on the INestApplication instance.

chapters.title: Raw body
chapters.summary: One of the most common reasons to access the raw request body is webhook signature verification.

chapters.title: Hybrid application
chapters.summary: A hybrid application listens for requests from two or more different sources.

chapters.summary: Nest applications handle requests and produce responses in a sequence called the request lifecycle.
